traveler: Shams al-Din Muhammad of Tabriz (Shams-e Tabrizi, Shams-e Parande)
title: The Flier: Forty Years of Looking, Forty Days Behind a Door, and Four Graves
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Tabriz, the Making of the Flier

stops.name: Tabriz, the birth without a year
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no primary source states a birth year; circa 1185 is counted backward from a death itself placed at 1247 or 1248
stops.campa: A son is born in Tabriz, in the Azerbaijan of the Seljuk Persian world, and no document records the day. The year is arrived at backward, by subtracting a traditional age at death from a death that is itself disputed. They call him Shams al-Din Muhammad, the Sun of the Faith. Everything known about the first sixty years of his life will pass through devotional compilers working a century later; the man himself leaves only sayings, and the sayings keep no calendar.
suggested_refs: The Mevlevi biographical corpus (Sepahsalar, Sultan Walad, Aflaki), sole carrier of the pre-Konya life
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Tabriz, the father whose name the sources do not agree on
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the childhood is undated in every source
stops.campa: Sepahsalar's Resaleh calls him son of Imam Ala al-Din. Aflaki's Manaqib al-Arifin names the father Ali and the grandfather Malikdad, and the Turkish tradition carries the full form Shams al-Din Muhammad bin Ali bin Malikdad Tabrizi. The two earliest biographical traditions of the Mevlevi order thus give one man two different fathers, and neither can be checked against the other. Both are recorded here and neither is resolved. Sepahsalar wrote a generation after the death, Aflaki a century after that, and no Tabriz document of the period survives to arbitrate between them.
suggested_refs: Sepahsalar, Resaleh; Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin, on the paternal name

stops.name: Tabriz, the workshop of Abu Bakr Sallabaf
stops.date_confidence: traditional: Turkish sources give the service as fourteen years beginning at age twenty-two, against an uncertain birth year
stops.campa: At twenty-two he attaches himself to Abu Bakr Sallabaf, the basket-weaver of Tabriz, a shaykh of the futuwwa and Malamati current who holds no chair and writes no book. Turkish tradition gives the service as fourteen years. No source locates the workshop and no stone of it survives, so the pin sits on the city and claims nothing finer. Later accounts hand Shams the master's craft as his own trade, basket-weaving and the selling of girdles, while other manuscripts call him zarduz, the embroiderer.
suggested_refs: The futuwwa and Malamati craft-guild Sufism of thirteenth-century Tabriz
sources: William C. Chittick, introduction to Me and Rumi

stops.name: Tabriz, the teachers whose lists do not match
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no source dates the schooling, and the sources disagree on who taught him and where
stops.campa: Persian sources name Pir Sele-baf, Shams Khunji and Shaykh Rukn al-Din Sujasi among his masters, and Sujas lies near Zanjan, not in Tabriz. Turkish sources add Salahaddin Mahmud. English encyclopedias insert a Baba Kamal al-Din Jumdi who exists under that spelling nowhere else: the man is Baba Kamal al-Din Jandi, of Jand on the Syr Darya, a Kubrawi in the line of Najm al-Din Kubra, and no Tabriz master at all. No two of the lists agree, and between them they put the schooling in Tabriz, near Zanjan and on the Syr Darya at once.
suggested_refs: Baba Kamal al-Din Jandi of Jand, Kubrawi shaykh, misspelled Jumdi in English reference works

stops.name: Tabriz, the Flier leaves
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the departure is undated in every source and inferred from the fourteen years of service
stops.campa: He goes, and does not settle again. The epithet the tradition fixes on him is Shams-e Parande, Shams the Flier, given because he never stays anywhere long enough to be found twice at one address. He travels with no lodge behind him and no chain of authority to invoke. He takes no students. In the Maqalat he says plainly what he was after on those roads: not a teacher and not a doctrine, but one companion able to bear his company for longer than an evening.
suggested_refs: The epithet Shams-e Parande, preserved in Mevlevi biographical tradition

stops.name: Isfahan, a city that is only a name in the record
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the Maqalat fixes no chronology for the wandering years and the order of cities is not established
stops.campa: Isfahan appears in secondary accounts of the wandering decades as a stop on the circuit, and nothing else appears with it: no lodge, no master, no year, no anecdote. The Maqalat, which is Shams speaking in his own voice, gives no itinerary that can be laid on a map in order. This pin marks a claim of presence and admits it carries no detail. It is the first of several such pins. The city is entered because a later writer put it in a list, and no earlier writer put it anywhere.
suggested_refs: Secondary accounts of Shams's pre-Konya circuit, unverified against primary sources
sources: Secondary biographical mentions of Shams's itinerant decades (not independently verified)

stops.name: Baghdad, the lodges of the old city
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: Baghdad is named in the Maqalat, the year is not
stops.campa: Baghdad stands in the Maqalat among the cities he passed through, and secondary tradition moves him among its Sufi circles, including those touched by the Suhrawardi order. No Baghdad text names a khanqah he entered or a shaykh he sat with. Eight years before, a boy from Balkh had spent thirty days here at the tomb of Junayd al-Baghdadi while his father Baha al-Din Walad carried the household west ahead of the Mongols. That boy is Jalal al-Din, now lecturing on law in Konya, and the two men have not met.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Junayd al-Baghdadi and the Suhrawardi lodges of thirteenth-century Baghdad
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Damascus, the passage before Konya
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: an earlier Damascus visit is traditional, undated, and unverified against a primary citation
stops.campa: Damascus takes him in for the first time, decades before it will hide him. A persistent tradition sets him against the city's Sufi elite here and has him dismissing Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi as a man of intellect rather than a lover of God; no primary citation for the remark has been produced. Ibn Arabi is alive in this city and will die in it in 1240, buried on the slope of Qasiyun. Whether the two men ever stood in one room, no source says, and the tradition that supplies the insult supplies no occasion for it.
suggested_refs: The Damascus Sufi milieu of Ibn Arabi and Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi in the 1230s
sources: Secondary Rumi and Shams biographies (Ibn Arabi remark unconfirmed)

stops.name: Mecca, a pilgrimage on weak attestation
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the hajj rests on diffuse hagiographic strands, with no specific primary citation located
stops.campa: Some later hagiographic strands credit the Flier with a hajj somewhere in the wandering years. The attestation is unspecific and no primary source names the season or the year. The Kaaba enters his story more securely by another route: the paradox of Abu Yazid al-Bistami, who went round the House and did not see the Lord of the House, only the House, is the paradox Shams will fire at a professor in a Konya street. The stone is inherited from Bayazid's journey, not from any documented pilgrimage of his own.
suggested_refs: Abu Yazid al-Bistami's circumambulation of the Kaaba, the paradox Shams invokes at Konya
sources: Diffuse hagiographic tradition; no specific citation located

stops.name: Aleppo, the citadel district
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: Aleppo is named in the tradition without a year
stops.campa: Aleppo is named among the cities of the wandering years and sketched by later biographers in outline only. It sits on the road between the Levant and the Seljuk marches of Anatolia, and every account that carries him north carries him through it. Jalal al-Din had studied here at the Halawiyya madrasa in the same decade, and here too the paths do not touch. No register in Aleppo records his arrival and no chronicle his departure. He is placed here because the road places him here.
suggested_refs: The Halawiyya madrasa of Aleppo, where Rumi studied in the 1230s
sources: Secondary biographical consensus on Shams's pre-Konya travels

stops.name: Erzincan, into the Seljuk marches
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the eastern Anatolian towns are named without dates
stops.campa: The Maqalat names Erzurum and Erzincan among the towns of the eastern Anatolian passage. The coordinate is a modern town center, because no building in either place is attached to him by any source consulted. Sixteen years earlier the Malika Ismati Khatun had kept Baha al-Din Walad's household in this same town on their long flight west. The corridor that is emptying Khorasan of its scholars is the corridor Shams now walks in the opposite temper, alone, with nothing to carry and no household behind him.
suggested_refs: Erzincan under the patronage of the Malika Ismati Khatun, waypoint of the Khorasani exodus

stops.name: Sivas, transit
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: a name in a list, unverified against any primary source
stops.campa: Sivas belongs to the same loosely attested circuit, a name in a list of names. The Anatolia he crosses is Seljuk, sultan-patronized, thick with madrasas endowed by amirs and with dervishes of every stripe walking between them. It is a country in which a man of no lineage and no license can move for years without once being written down. Shams moves through it for years and no Seljuk register catches him. The stop is carried by secondary tradition alone, with no primary source behind it.
suggested_refs: The Seljuk madrasa network of thirteenth-century central Anatolia
sources: Secondary tradition on Shams's Anatolian route (unverified)

stops.name: Kayseri, the quarrel with Awhad al-Din Kirmani
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: accounts place the meeting variously at Kayseri, at Konya, or nowhere in particular
stops.campa: Tradition sets an encounter with the elder Sufi Awhad al-Din Kirmani somewhere on this circuit, and the accounts do not agree where. In the Maqalat Shams speaks of Kirmani with contempt, faulting his practice of contemplating the divine beauty in the faces of handsome youths. It is the one doctrinal quarrel of the wandering years preserved in his own voice. Kirmani belongs to Ibn Arabi's circle, which is the second time that circle stands across the Flier's road without anyone recording a meeting.
suggested_refs: Awhad al-Din Kirmani and the contested practice of shahid-bazi, contemplation of beauty in created forms
sources: Widely repeated secondary tradition (city of meeting unfixed)

stops.name: Aksaray, the last stage before Konya
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the approach to Konya is traditional and undated
stops.campa: Aksaray is the town tradition assigns to the final approach, the last stage of a search that has run for decades through Baghdad, Damascus, Aleppo, Erzurum, Sivas and Kayseri. He is near sixty. He has asked in every city for a companion capable of enduring him and has not found one. Two days of road to the west lies Konya, where a professor of jurisprudence keeps a madrasa, a pulpit, a household, and a reputation for orthodoxy that has never once been disturbed.
stops.quote: What will you give in return? ... My head! ... The one you seek is Jalal ud-Din of Konya.
stops.quote_source: The vision-dialogue of Shams's search, as rendered in the English Wikipedia article 'Rumi' from the Sufi hagiographic tradition
suggested_refs: The Aksaray road, last stage of the approach to the Seljuk capital
sources: Secondary tradition on Shams's approach to Konya (unverified)

stops.name: Konya, the Inn of the Sugar Merchants
stops.date_confidence: attested to 26 Jumada al-Thani 642 AH, converting to 29 November 1244 Julian; the 15 November date in English reference works is a bad conversion of the same Islamic date
stops.campa: A man dressed head to foot in black felt takes a room at the Inn of the Sugar Merchants, the Khan al-Shakariyya, and gives nobody a name that means anything. The Persian tradition fixes the day: the twenty-sixth of Jumada al-Thani, 642. He has walked into the seat of the Seljuk sultanate, a city the household of Baha al-Din Walad reached fifteen years before him as refugees from Balkh, and he has come for exactly one man in it. The accounts split on how they first meet: one has him seizing a bridle in the square, another has him finding the professor at work among his books.
stops.quote_source: Shams's opening words to Rumi in a variant account of the first encounter, English Wikipedia article 'Shams Tabrizi'
suggested_refs: The Khan al-Shakariyya (Sekerciler Han), Konya, Shams's lodging on arrival

stops.name: Konya, the question in the street
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the scene is hagiographic elaboration in Aflaki and Sultan Walad, not a documented event
stops.campa: He takes the bridle of Jalal al-Din's mount in the square and asks which is greater, the Prophet Muhammad who said we have not known You as You should be known, or Abu Yazid al-Bistami who said glory be to me, how great is my station. The tradition has the professor go off the horse in a faint. Bayazid's boast is the same one the Baghdad jurists tried him for four centuries earlier; Shams uses it as a door, and a man who has taught law for twenty years walks through it.
stops.quote: which is greater, the Prophet Muhammad, who said, we have not known You, God, as You should be known, or Bayazid Bistami, who said, glory be to me, how great is my station?
stops.quote_source: The question at the first meeting, transmitted in Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin, and Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama
suggested_refs: Bayazid Bastami's ecstatic utterance and its four-century afterlife in Sufi controversy

stops.name: Konya, the forty days behind the locked door
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the count of forty days is Mevlevi tradition, with no contemporary record
stops.campa: Rumi takes him into his own household and the two shut themselves in a cell for forty days. Food goes in through the door; nothing comes out. No disciple is admitted, and no member of the family. What passes between them in those weeks is recorded nowhere by either man, and the Mevlevi order has kept the silence as carefully as it has kept the count of days. When the door opens, the professor of Konya has stopped being a professor, and the Flier has found what he spent forty years on the roads asking for.
suggested_refs: The forty-day chilla of seclusion in Sufi practice, and the Mevlevi memory of this one

stops.name: Konya, the pulpit abandoned
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the change is attested by Sultan Walad and Aflaki without a date
stops.campa: Jalal al-Din puts down the law lectures and the muftiship. Students who queued for his rulings find the chair empty and the man in it turning to music. Sultan Walad, twenty years old and watching from inside the house, will write the change down decades later in the Ibtidanama, which is the nearest thing to an eyewitness the whole affair possesses. His father is famous, endowed, and the son of the Sultan of the Scholars. He has traded all of it for the company of a stranger out of Tabriz.
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama, the earliest and closest account of Rumi's transformation

stops.name: Konya, a city thick with jurists takes offense
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the hostility is attested in outline, its onset undated
stops.campa: Konya under the house of Kayqubad is a capital of competing schools, jurists, poets and dervishes drawn west by Mongol pressure on Khorasan. Its learned circle knows exactly what a teacher is worth and exactly what papers one carries. Shams has none: no chain of authority, no madrasa, no license, no book. The charge against him is not heresy but nullity, the outrage that the city's greatest scholar has been captured by a man with nothing to show. The murmuring starts inside the household and spreads outward from there.
suggested_refs: Konya under Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad I, refuge of the scholars fleeing the Mongol advance
sources: rumi.journey.json, 'Konya, arrival at the sultan's invitation' (1229)

segments.name: The First Flight and the Return

stops.name: Konya, the murmuring reaches the door
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the atlas's own rumi entry dates the murmuring to January 1246; Sultan Walad gives no date
stops.campa: Resentment settles into something with a direction. Disciples who had been the professor's own now count the stranger a thief, and the household adds its grievance to theirs. Sultan Walad's chronicle names the hostility without naming who spoke it, which is as close as a son can come to accusing his father's students in writing. Shams, who has spent forty years reading rooms where he was not wanted, reads this one early. He says nothing to Rumi about leaving and makes no arrangement anyone can afterward point to.
stops.quote: A good man complains of no-one; he does not look to faults.
stops.quote_source: Maqalat-e Shams-e Tabrizi, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Shams Tabrizi'
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama, on the disciples' hostility to Shams
sources: rumi.journey.json, 'the disciples murmur, Shams reads the danger' (1246-01-01)

stops.name: Konya, the departure without warning
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 Shawwal 643 AH, converting to 11 March 1246 Julian; the atlas's own rumi entry places the flight three weeks earlier at 1246-02-15
stops.campa: He goes out of Konya without notice and without farewell. The one man in the city who would have stopped him is not told. The Persian tradition dates it to the twenty-first of Shawwal, 643. Nobody sees which road he takes. For the second time in his life the Flier proves the epithet, and this time the flight costs someone else more than it costs him: the household that wanted him gone gets what it wanted, and finds it has broken the man it meant to protect.
suggested_refs: The dating of the first flight to 21 Shawwal 643 AH in the Persian tradition

stops.name: Damascus, refuge in the Umayyad quarter
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the refuge is attested, the month of arrival is not
stops.campa: He surfaces in Damascus, in the quarter around the great Umayyad mosque, and stays. It is the city Jalal al-Din studied in as a young man and the city where Ibn Arabi has lain six years under Mount Qasiyun. Letters go out from Konya in every direction asking after a man in black felt. Damascus is large, its khanqahs are many, and a wanderer who has spent decades not being written down is not easily found in it. He does not send word to Konya, and he does not go home to Tabriz either.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque quarter of Damascus, Shams's refuge in the first flight

stops.name: Konya, the grief the order records as an illness
stops.date_confidence: traditional: Sultan Walad describes the grief without giving its duration
stops.campa: Rumi stops speaking. He composes verses and destroys them. He turns students from the door and keeps a silence the Mevlevi tradition describes in the vocabulary of sickness rather than of mourning. The men who drove Shams out watch the result and do not repeat the experiment for a year and a half. Sultan Walad, writing it down, gives no measure of how long the silence runs. The house that could not tolerate the stranger now arranges itself around his absence.
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama, on Rumi's grief during the first absence

stops.name: Damascus, found by the son
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the year rests on the atlas's own rumi entry; English reference works give the errand without any date
stops.campa: Sultan Walad rides to Damascus with his father's verse-letters and finds him. He is twenty or twenty-one, born at Larende in April 1226, a grown man and not the boy the later retellings make of him. He delivers the letters and argues his father's case in a city that owes him nothing. Shams agrees to come back. On the return road the son refuses the offered horse and walks the last miles on foot beside Shams's mount, and the man who sets that detail down in the Ibtidanama is the man who did it.
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama, the eyewitness account of the Damascus errand
sources: rumi.journey.json, 'Sultan Walad rides to bring him home' (1247-04-01)

stops.name: Konya, the reunion
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the atlas's own rumi entry places the return at April 1247; the month is not independently fixed
stops.campa: The two meet in front of the city. Sultan Walad's account has both men going down, each at the other's feet, and the onlookers unable to say afterward which of them fell first. It is the only scene in the whole story the crowd of Konya witnesses together, and the only one for which the earliest source is a participant rather than a compiler. Whatever the household has learned in the fourteen months of silence, it has not learned to want Shams back inside its walls.
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama, on the reunion of Rumi and Shams, April 1247

stops.name: Konya, the discourses taken down
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the Maqalat is undated and its compilation is placed loosely in the Konya years
stops.campa: Disciples begin writing down what he says. The result is the Maqalat, Persian prose in Shams's own voice: his impatience with jurisprudence, his forty years of looking for an equal, his private judgment of Rumi, his instruction not to be content with being a faqih or even a Sufi but to want more than whatever stands in front of you. He does not compose it. He talks, the room copies, and that is the only book he leaves, assembled from notes by hands other than his.
stops.quote: Don't be content with being a faqih (religious scholar), say I want more – more than being a Sufi (a mystic), more than being a mystic – more than each thing that comes before you.
stops.quote_source: Maqalat-e Shams-e Tabrizi, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Shams Tabrizi'
suggested_refs: The Maqalat-e Shams-e Tabrizi, compiled from disciples' notes rather than authored as a treatise
sources: William C. Chittick, introduction to Me and Rumi

stops.name: Konya, the marriage to Kimya Khatun
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the year is carried by the tradition and by the atlas's own rumi entry; the month is not fixed
stops.campa: To fix him in the city, Rumi marries him to Kimya Khatun, a girl raised in Rumi's own household as a foster child. The commonly repeated detail that she is the daughter of Rumi's second wife Kerra Khatun by an earlier marriage is carried by no reference work checked in Turkish, Persian or English, and stands here as unsupported. The marriage is a fastening, not a match: a man who has never stayed anywhere is given a wife in the one house that wants him gone. It hands the household a new grievance instead of settling the old one.
suggested_refs: Kimya Khatun, foster child of Rumi's household, married to Shams in 1247
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, what he says while the house closes in
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the sayings are undated and placed here by their Konya setting
stops.campa: In the Maqalat he says the meaning of the Book of God is not the text but the man who guides: he is the Book of God, he is its verses, he is scripture. He speaks of Persian as holding an elegance Arabic does not, of joy as clear water where wondrous blossoms grow and sorrow as a black flood that wilts them, of a good man as one who complains of nobody and does not look for faults. The voice is plain, abrupt, and entirely unconcerned with the schools now working to expel him.
stops.quote: The meaning of the Book of God is not the text, it is the man who guides. He is the Book of God, he is its verses, he is scripture.
stops.quote_source: Maqalat-e Shams-e Tabrizi, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Shams Tabrizi'
suggested_refs: The Maqalat's doctrine of the guiding man as the living scripture

stops.name: Konya, Kimya fails
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the sequence of Kimya's death relative to the disappearance is inconsistent across the traditional accounts
stops.campa: Accounts describe her health declining under the pressure of a house that will not accept her husband, and place her death close to Shams's own disappearance without agreeing which came first. Franklin Lewis, weighing the tradition, finds the chronology unfixable. She is the one person in the story with no voice in any source: no saying preserved, no chronicle written by a son. She is recorded here where the tradition puts her, and the order of the two deaths is left unsorted.
stops.quote: Joy is like pure clear water; wherever it flows, wondrous blossoms grow…Sorrow is like a black flood; wherever it flows it wilts the blossoms.
stops.quote_source: Maqalat-e Shams-e Tabrizi, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Shams Tabrizi'
suggested_refs: Franklin Lewis on the unresolved chronology of Kimya Khatun's death
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, called to the door
stops.date_confidence: traditional: Turkish sources give 645 AH, which runs 8 May 1247 to 26 April 1248, so a December inside it can only be 1247; the 5 December 1248 date in English reference works is the outlier
stops.campa: On a night in early winter someone calls him from the back door while he and Rumi are talking. He says, in the words the tradition keeps, that he is called to be killed. He goes out into the dark of the courtyard. Nobody sees him alive again, and nobody in Konya produces a body, a grave, a killer or a witness. Sultan Walad, who was in the house that night, who wrote the fullest early account of everything else, and who had once ridden to Damascus to fetch him home, records no death at all.
stops.quote: I am called to be killed.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Shams of Tabriz on the night of his disappearance (Mevlevi oral tradition, later Ottoman-era chroniclers)
suggested_refs: The silence of Sultan Walad's Ibtidanama on Shams's fate, against the later murder narrative
sources: Mevlevi oral tradition and Ottoman-era chroniclers
rumi.journey.json, 'the last night, the cry in the dark' (1247-12-05)

stops.name: Konya, the seven men and the well
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the murder narrative is a later accretion, absent from the earliest source
stops.campa: Later tradition names seven men implicated by rumor, and in some versions puts Rumi's second son Ala al-Din among them. It holds that a body was found in a well near the house and buried in the night. None of this is in the Ibtidanama. Modern scholarship reading Aflaki against Sultan Walad treats the murder as dramatization layered onto an original silence, and allows the flat alternative: that the Flier flew, resumed the life he had led for forty years, and died elsewhere of nothing in particular.
suggested_refs: Franklin Lewis on the reliability of Aflaki and the accretion of the murder narrative
sources: Later Mevlevi and Ottoman-era oral tradition
Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the rose garden
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the quiet burial is a counter-tradition with no marker and no witness
stops.campa: A counter-tradition buries him quietly beside Baha al-Din Walad, in the rose garden Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad gave the family for the father's grave, later domed as the Kubbe-i Hadra. If it is true, Shams lies under the Green Dome with the two men whose house he came to Konya to break open: the Sultan of the Scholars, who never met him, and Jalal al-Din, who will be laid there twenty-five years later. The tradition offers no marker, no witness, and no date.
suggested_refs: The Kubbe-i Hadra (Green Dome) over the sultan's rose garden, Konya
sources: Mevlevi tradition; local Konya shrine veneration

stops.name: Konya, the Makam-i Shems
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the shrine's foundation is not established; the date is a placeholder and the coordinate is the standing Sems-i Tebrizi mosque and turbe
stops.campa: Seven hundred metres northwest of the Green Dome, in the quarter that now carries his name, stands the Sems-i Tebrizi mosque and turbe, venerated as the Makam-i Shems. The cenotaph inside is modest, and Turkish sources concede that what it holds, if anything, is uncertain even in local tradition. It is a second Konya pin for a man who has no confirmed first one. Pilgrims reach it and the Green Dome on the same afternoon, and pray at both without deciding between them.
suggested_refs: Sems-i Tebrizi Camii ve Turbesi, Semsitebrizi Mahallesi, Karatay, Konya (Wikidata Q131390887)

stops.name: Khoy, the tradition of a natural death
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the eastern tradition places the death in 1248 and cannot be reconciled with the Konya accounts
stops.campa: A tradition running against everything in the Konya accounts holds that he was never murdered: that he left the city under his own power, traveled east, settled at Khoy in West Azerbaijan and died there of age, at sixty-two or sixty-three. The two stories cannot both be true and no source reconciles them. Khoy lies a few days' ride from the Tabriz he was born in, which makes the eastern version a homecoming and the Konya version an execution, built out of the same set of facts.
suggested_refs: The Khoy tradition of Shams's departure from Konya and natural death

stops.name: Khoy, the tomb and the tower
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the standing monument is modern and the identification of the grave rests on local tradition; the date is a placeholder
stops.campa: Two kilometres northwest of the town, in a memorial park beside a tall tower monument, a grave is maintained as his and shown to visitors. Iran has put the complex forward for UNESCO World Heritage listing. Three Timurid-era skeletons were found near the minaret, which dates the site's use as a burial ground and settles nothing about whose bones lie in the grave. Konya and Khoy both keep pilgrimage to a tomb of the same man, eleven hundred kilometres apart.
suggested_refs: Tomb of Shams Tabrizi, Zeynali, Khoy (Wikidata Q16044966); the Timurid skeletons found near the minaret

stops.name: Tabriz, the Gecil cemetery claim
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the site could not be matched to any surviving cemetery; both date and coordinate are placeholders
stops.campa: Turkish sources list a third grave, in the Tabriz cemetery they name Gecil, which would return him to the city he left sixty years earlier. No surviving cemetery has been matched to that name in anything reachable, and the coordinate is an approximate placement in the old burial district, unverified. It is offered here as a claim and not as a location. It is the third city to claim him, after Konya and Khoy, and no source places a body in any of them.
suggested_refs: Turkish Wikipedia's list of claimed burial sites, including 'Tebriz, Gecil mezarligi'

stops.name: Nigde, the Tomb of the Beheaded
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: a local attribution with no date; the coordinate is the town center rather than the turbe
stops.campa: A local tradition in Nigde attaches the Kesikbas Turbesi, the Tomb of the Beheaded, to him, which implies a beheading, a manner of death fitting none of the other accounts. The coordinate is the town center and not the turbe itself, which could not be matched to any mapping source. Four graves now stand for one body, at Konya, Khoy, Tabriz and here, each with its own manner of dying attached, and the founding chronicle of the order records none of them.
suggested_refs: Kesikbas Turbesi, Nigde, listed among the claimed sites

stops.name: Multan, the shrine of Shah Shams Tabrez
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: a folk conflation with a historically distinct and probably later Multan saint; the date is a placeholder
stops.campa: A major shrine in Multan is venerated as the tomb of a Shah Shams Tabrez, and popular devotion in the Punjab identifies him with Rumi's companion. The historical consensus is that the Multan saint is a different and probably later Sufi who shares a nisba. The conflation is recorded here rather than quietly resolved. The nisba travelled as far as the Indus, and a shrine was raised where it arrived. Popular devotion has not distinguished the two men since.
suggested_refs: The Multan shrine of Shah Shams Tabrez and its conflation with Rumi's companion

stops.name: Damascus, the two searches and the turning inward
stops.date_confidence: traditional: Aflaki and Lewis carry the two searches; the months are not fixed
stops.campa: Refusing to believe it, Rumi rides to Damascus himself, twice, working through the quarters and the khanqahs asking after him. The city that sheltered Shams in the first flight gives up nothing in the second. Somewhere in that search the looking stops: why should I seek, he says, I am the same as He, His essence speaks through me, I have been looking for myself. The man who came to Konya to find one companion has been absorbed into the one he found.
stops.quote: Why should I seek? I am the same as He. His essence speaks through me. I have been looking for myself.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Rumi's realization in Damascus, within the transmitted teaching of the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi
suggested_refs: Rumi's two Damascus searches, and the abandonment of the outward search
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Konya, the goldsmith who came after
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the atlas's own rumi entry dates Salah al-Din Zarkub's companionship from 1249
stops.campa: In Shams's place Rumi takes Salah al-Din Zarkub, an illiterate goldsmith, and keeps him ten years. Where Shams was fire, the goldsmith is a steady coal. After him comes Husam al-Din Chelebi, introduced in the Mevlevi accounts as the hand that catches what burns, and the Masnavi is dictated to him. Every companion Rumi takes for the rest of his life is described by the order in terms of the one who disappeared. The house that had wanted the stranger gone goes on measuring by him.
suggested_refs: Salah al-Din Zarkub and Husam al-Din Chelebi, the second and third companions
sources: rumi.journey.json, Salah al-Din Zarkub and Husam al-Din Chelebi stops

stops.name: Konya, forty thousand verses in another man's name
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the Divan accumulates across decades and has no date of composition
stops.campa: Rumi begins signing his lyrics Shams-e Tabrizi. The collection runs past forty thousand verses across more than three thousand ghazals, mostly Persian with lines of Arabic, Turkish and Greek, and students gather it after his death as the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi. Not one line of it is Shams's writing. It is a poet putting another man's name where his own signature belongs, and he does it for twenty-five years. Shams leaves one book he did not write; Rumi leaves him a second.
stops.quote: O Shamsi Tabriz, beauty and glory of the horizons, / What king but is a beggar of thee with heart and soul?
stops.quote_source: Divan-i Shamsi Tabriz, tr. Reynold A. Nicholson, 'Selections from the Divani Shamsi Tabriz'
suggested_refs: The Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi (Divan-i Kabir), Foruzanfar's 1957 critical edition
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West
Reynold A. Nicholson, Selections from the Divani Shamsi Tabriz (1898)

stops.name: Konya, the son keeps the story straight
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the atlas's own rumi entry dates Sultan Walad's formalization of the order to 1284
stops.campa: Sultan Walad, the man who rode to Damascus, formalizes the sema into fixed movements and writes the Ibtidanama and the Rabab-nama for pupils who never saw Shams. His is the founding document and the only near-eyewitness the tradition possesses, and on the question of how Shams died he writes nothing. Aflaki, compiling the Manaqib al-Arifin two generations later, supplies the well, the seven men and the knife. The order has carried both versions ever since without choosing.
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad's Ibtidanama and Rabab-nama, and the formalization of the sema

stops.name: Tehran, the discourses put in order
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Mohammad-Ali Movahhed publishes a two-volume critical Persian edition of the Maqalat with Khwarazmi in Tehran, seven hundred years after the disciples took the notes. William Chittick renders it into English in 2004 as Me and Rumi: The Autobiography of Shams-i Tabrizi, the first substantial passage of Shams's own voice, as against Rumi's poems about him, into another language. The book that was never written by its author finally has an apparatus.
suggested_refs: Movahhed's two-volume Maqalat (Khwarazmi, Tehran, 1990); Chittick, Me and Rumi (Fons Vitae, 2004)
sources: William C. Chittick, Me and Rumi: The Autobiography of Shams-i Tabrizi (2004)

stops.name: Khoy, the nomination
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the UNESCO nomination is a process without a single fixed date; the year is a placeholder
stops.campa: Iran forwards the tomb complex at Khoy for UNESCO World Heritage listing, which obliges a state to assert as fact what the sources have refused to settle for seven centuries. In the same decades Elif Shafak's The Forty Rules of Love sells past three quarters of a million copies in Turkey and France and enters the BBC's list of the hundred most influential novels. No contemporary portrait or description of the man survives to correct anyone; the black felt and the wandering figure are a later painter's invention.
suggested_refs: The UNESCO World Heritage nomination of the Khoy tomb complex; Elif Shafak, The Forty Rules of Love (2009)
